clue.text: Stout fella's proverbial title (5)

parts.note: Rex Stout's fifth Nero Wolfe novel takes its title from the proverb about too many people spoiling the broth

explanation.surface: Someone praises a portly chap for living up to a well-known saying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stout' looks like an adjective for a fat fellow, but it is Rex Stout, American detective writer; the (5) points to his fifth Nero Wolfe book.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel's title is the first half of the saying about cooks who spoil the broth.

clue.text: One of Farrell's difficulties

parts.note: J. G. Farrell wrote the Irish novel ..., so a single difficulty is one of his title's plural

explanation.surface: A reader lists the problems facing someone called Farrell.
explanation.walkthrough: J. G. Farrell's novel Troubles (1970) is set in Ireland in 1919-21; take one of those troubles.
explanation.definitionFit: A single difficulty or worry is the singular of the Farrell title.

clue.text: Circular contribution to Greek letters

parts.note: the round letter of the Greek alphabet is the 'little o', so a circular shape is its contribution

explanation.surface: Someone sends a round-robin article to a journal of Greek scholarship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circular' suggests a leaflet sent round and 'Greek letters' a literary field; it is the round Greek letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the fifteenth letter of the Greek alphabet, a short o drawn as a circle.

clue.text: Fragrant nosegay (from Palgrave, for example)

parts.note: the Greek root means a gathering of flowers, and Palgrave's Golden Treasury is a famous collection of poems

explanation.surface: A sweet-smelling posy is handed over by someone called Palgrave.
explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from Greek for 'flower-gathering'; F. T. Palgrave compiled The Golden Treasury, a Victorian poetry collection.
explanation.definitionFit: A collection of chosen poems is literally a bouquet of flowers in its Greek origin.

clue.text: Poet, say, or novelist as yet unrecognized

indicators.note: letters that cannot be recognized are disguised, so the words as yet are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a writer is a poet or a novelist not yet famous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unrecognized' rearranges AS YET. 'Poet, say' is a bonus: the poet W. B. Yeats sounds the same as Richard Yates, the American novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Yates was the American writer of Revolutionary Road.

clue.text: Shandy for a servant? on the contrary

definitions.text: Shandy for a servant? on the contrary

parts.words: Shandy for a servant? on the contrary
parts.note: turned round, the clue asks for a servant of the Shandy family in Sterne's novel

explanation.surface: A pub-goer asks whether a beer-and-lemonade drink is suitable for the staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shandy' looks like the drink, but it is Sterne's Tristram Shandy; reversing the request gives the Shandys' manservant.
explanation.definitionFit: In Tristram Shandy the household manservant of Walter Shandy has this Old Testament name.

clue.text: Lime made a comeback in his best known work

definitions.text: Lime made a comeback in his best known work

parts.words: Lime made a comeback in his best known work
parts.note: the word lime written backwards gives the boy hero of a famous German children's book about detectives

explanation.surface: A fruit, or perhaps Harry Lime, returns in some author's most famous work.
explanation.walkthrough: LIME reversed is EMIL, of Emil and the Detectives by the German writer Erich Kästner.
explanation.definitionFit: Erich Kästner, German author, is best known for Emil and the Detectives.

clue.text: Pinnacle of existence, due to brain work, they say

definitions.meaning: the high point of living, being at the summit of one's career

definitions.text: due to brain work, they say
definitions.meaning: brain sounds like John Braine, whose sequel to Room at the Top has this title

explanation.surface: Success in life, someone claims, comes from intellectual effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brain work' sounds like 'Braine work': John Braine, English novelist, wrote this sequel to Room at the Top.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means the existence enjoyed by those who have reached the peak of success, and is also Braine's novel title.

clue.text: Press "first" for satirical writer

parts.note: to press clothes is to iron them
first is abbreviated 1st, read as the letters IST

explanation.surface: Someone is told to hit the first button to reach a satirist.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1 of 1ST is read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who uses irony, saying the opposite of what is meant, writes satire.

clue.text: Tristan perhaps in it when returning to Cornwall

definitions.text: in it when returning to Cornwall

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the name Tristan might be some other arrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: Tristan seems to be part of something on his journey back to Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges TRISTAN. In the legend Tristan was travelling, in transit, when he brought Isolde back to King Mark in Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone travelling between places is in transit, as Tristan was on his voyage.

clue.text: Ballet about song producer

definitions.meaning: a famous solo dance choreographed by Fokine for Pavlova
a dying swan is supposed to sing its swan song

explanation.surface: A dance piece about someone who makes records.
explanation.walkthrough: Legend says a swan sings only as it dies, hence a 'swan song'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fokine's short ballet for Pavlova to Saint-Saëns has this title, and the legendary bird sings as it dies.

clue.text: Prohibition (some of them bar good books).

indicators.note: only some of the letters of these words are taken, a run sitting inside them

explanation.surface: A ban: certain people exclude worthy books.
explanation.definitionFit: An official ban on trade is a prohibition.

clue.text: Snow culture (one of two)

parts.note: C. P. Snow's lecture The Two Cultures set the arts against another field of knowledge

explanation.surface: Someone describes a winter way of life, one of a pair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snow' is C. P. Snow, whose 1959 lecture The Two Cultures contrasted literary and scientific thought.
explanation.definitionFit: Snow's two cultures were the humanities and the physical and natural disciplines of research.

clue.text: Media connection including accessory

parts.note: a tie is a clothing accessory
in can mean including, as in 'tax in'

explanation.surface: A link to the press involves some piece of fashion kit.
explanation.definitionFit: A product linked to a film or programme is a tie-in.

clue.text: Aran islander nominally gets return of mail

definitions.text: Aran islander nominally gets return of mail

parts.words: Aran islander nominally gets return of mail
parts.note: the Irish writer Liam, born on Inishmore, bears a surname that names him

explanation.surface: Someone on the Aran Islands receives a returned letter.
explanation.walkthrough: Liam O'Flaherty, Irish novelist, was born on Inishmore in the Aran Islands.
explanation.definitionFit: Liam O'Flaherty was the Aran-born author of The Informer.

clue.text: Novelist to join subsequently

parts.note: to link is to join
later means subsequently

explanation.surface: A writer is set to team up at a later date.
explanation.walkthrough: Eric Linklater was a Scottish novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric Linklater wrote Juan in America and other comic fiction.

clue.text: When the ——' peasant meets the he-bear in his pride" (Kipling)

definitions.text: When the ——' peasant meets the he-bear in his pride" (Kipling)

parts.words: When the ——' peasant meets the he-bear in his pride" (Kipling)
parts.note: a line from Kipling's The Truce of the Bear, with the peasant's mountain homeland missing

explanation.surface: A quotation from Kipling about a peasant confronting a bear.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap is filled from Kipling's poem The Truce of the Bear.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word describes a peasant from the great mountain range north of India.

clue.text: Former Portuguese capital

parts.note: capital means money, and this is an old gold coin of Portugal

explanation.surface: A clue asks for a city that was once the seat of Portugal's government.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' suggests a city such as Coimbra; it means money, an old Portuguese gold coin.
explanation.definitionFit: This gold coin of Portugal circulated in England in the eighteenth century.

clue.text: Milk has curdled, perhaps, for a goddess of wealth and prosperity

definitions.text: a goddess of wealth and prosperity

indicators.note: curdled milk is spoilt and broken up, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Milk that has gone off is offered to a Hindu goddess.
explanation.definitionFit: Lakshmi is the Hindu deity of fortune, consort of Vishnu.

clue.text: Copy of Lear lent to school reveals Bulgarian-born author

indicators.note: reveals shows the run sitting within the words Lear lent

explanation.surface: Lending a copy of King Lear to a school uncovers a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Arlen, author of The Green Hat, was born in Bulgaria to Armenian parents.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Arlen was a Bulgarian-born Armenian writer of 1920s society novels.

clue.text: Broadcasters remove dress, upset gymnast

indicators.note: upset means the remaining letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: TV people take off their clothing and annoy an athlete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remove' takes the letters of DRESS out of BROADCASTERS, leaving BOACATR, which 'upset' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: An acrobat performs tumbling and balancing feats like a gymnast.

clue.text: He was discouraged from making loan

definitions.text: He was discouraged from making loan

parts.words: He was discouraged from making loan
parts.note: Polonius tells his son 'neither a borrower nor a lender be' in Hamlet

explanation.surface: A man was talked out of lending money.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet, Polonius advises his son, leaving for France, against lending.
explanation.definitionFit: Polonius's son in Hamlet receives the famous advice against lending.

clue.text: Pensive figure at the Hotel Biron

definitions.text: Pensive figure at the Hotel Biron

parts.words: Pensive figure at the Hotel Biron
parts.note: the Paris mansion houses the Rodin Museum and his famous seated bronze

explanation.surface: A thoughtful guest is spotted at a hotel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hotel' suggests guests; the Hôtel Biron is the Paris mansion that is now the Musée Rodin.
explanation.definitionFit: Rodin's bronze of a seated man deep in thought stands in the museum's garden.

clue.text: Ian McEwan wrote them at last

definitions.text: Ian McEwan wrote them at last

parts.words: Ian McEwan wrote them at last
parts.note: McEwan's first story collection is titled First Love, Last ceremonies

explanation.surface: A novelist finally completed some works.
explanation.walkthrough: McEwan's collection is First Love, Last Rites, so they come 'at last'; w-RITES also echoes 'wrote'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rites are ceremonies, the last word of McEwan's book title.

clue.text: Generosity of sizeable security force envisaged in Britain by Deighton

parts.note: sizeable means large

parts.words: security force envisaged in Britain by Deighton
parts.note: Len Deighton's novel SS-GB imagines the Nazi SS in occupied Britain

explanation.surface: A big-hearted police force imagined by a thriller writer.
explanation.walkthrough: SS-GB is Len Deighton's alternative history of a Nazi-occupied Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Largess is liberal giving, open-handed bounty.

clue.text: Gain reported by, for example

annotationWithheld.why: Gain reported by, for example (7): 'Gain reported' sounds like PROFIT, but 'by, for example' gives no sensible definition; a name (e.g. of a prophet) seems lost after 'by' in the OCR

clue.text: … disciple named —, which by interpretation is called Dorcas " (Acts)

definitions.text: … disciple named —, which by interpretation is called Dorcas " (Acts)

parts.words: … disciple named —, which by interpretation is called Dorcas " (Acts)
parts.note: Acts 9:36 names the woman of Joppa raised by Peter, giving her Aramaic name and its Greek equivalent

explanation.surface: A quotation from Acts about a disciple with two names.
explanation.walkthrough: Both names mean gazelle, one Aramaic and one Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aramaic name meaning gazelle belongs to the charitable woman of Joppa.

clue.text: Subdue rustic, unlikely conspirator down

indicators.note: unlikely signals these letters stand in an improbable order and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone improbable is plotting to suppress a country bumpkin.
explanation.walkthrough: Decius Brutus is one of the plotters against Caesar in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar; 'down' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: He is one of the men who plot Caesar's murder in Shakespeare's play.
